summary: Defines the /.well-known/ path prefix, a reserved place on a site where standard files and metadata can be found at predictable locations. It also set up a registry for names under that prefix. It is no longer current, because it was replaced by RFC 8615.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5785 carves out one reserved path on every web site, /.well-known/, for files that describe the site itself rather than its content. A specification that needs such a file registers a name with IANA first, which keeps two specifications from choosing the same path and keeps them from landing on a page the site already had.

questions: where to put site metadata files
how to register a well-known uri
subtitle: The reserved path prefix that lets a site publish one piece of standard information at a fixed address.

tldr.problem: Web protocols often need to fetch a site's policy or other metadata before making a request, and there was no agreed place to put it, so every protocol invented its own path and sometimes collided with pages a site already had.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the path prefix /.well-known/ for such files. Any specification that wants a well-known URI registers its name with IANA, so two specifications cannot claim the same path.
tldr.outcome: The prefix became the standard place for such files as security.txt and the security-related policy documents. RFC 5785 has been obsoleted by RFC 8615.

facts.label: Permitted schemes
facts.value: HTTP, HTTPS, or a scheme specified to use well-known URIs

today: RFC 5785 has been obsoleted by RFC 8615, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in April 2010 as a Standards Track document, and it updated RFCs 2616 and 2818.

sections.title: Why a Reserved Prefix
sections.content:
It is increasingly common for web-based protocols to require the discovery of policy or other information about a host, that is site-wide metadata, before making a request. The Robots Exclusion Protocol, for example, specifies a way for automated processes to obtain permission to access resources, and the Platform for Privacy Preferences tells user agents how to discover a privacy policy beforehand.

There are several ways to reach per-resource metadata, such as HTTP headers or WebDAV's PROPFIND method, but the perceived overhead of those, in terms of client-perceived latency or deployment difficulty, often rules them out in these situations. When that happens, it is common to designate a well-known location for the data so that it can be easily found. The drawback is that this risks collisions, both with other well-known locations and with pre-existing resources on the site.

The RFC addresses that by defining a path prefix for HTTP and HTTPS URIs, /.well-known/. Future specifications that need a resource for site-wide metadata can register their use, which avoids collisions and minimises the impingement on a site's own URI space.

The RFC's appendix answers the objections it anticipates. Well-known locations are, it admits, bad for the web in various reasons, both technical and social, but they are commonly used and their use is increasing, and this memo defines a sandbox for them that reduces the risk of collision. The prefix was chosen because it is short, descriptive and, according to search indices, not widely used. The impact on existing mechanisms such as P3P and robots.txt is nil until they choose to use the mechanism. Per-directory well-known locations were not defined because allowing every path segment to have one would raise the risk of colliding with an existing URI and would not scale well, being too chatty.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a shared convention, each protocol picks its own path, and a site can end up with a page that collides with the convention. Reserving one prefix and keeping a registry of the names inside it means a collision has to be somebody's mistake rather than everyone's.

sections.title: Appropriate Use of Well-Known URIs
sections.content:
There are a number of ways applications could use well-known URIs. However, in keeping with the Architecture of the World Wide Web, well-known URIs are not intended for general information retrieval or for the establishment of large URI namespaces on the web. They are designed to facilitate the discovery of information on a site when it is not practical to use other mechanisms: for example, when discovering policy that has to be evaluated before a resource is accessed, or when using multiple round trips is judged detrimental to performance.

The well-known URI space was created with the expectation that it would be used to make site-wide policy information and other metadata available directly, if sufficiently concise, or to provide references to other URIs that provide such metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: This is for one small file per site, fetched once before something else happens, not for a filing system or a place to put everything a site publishes.

sections.title: What Counts as a Well-Known URI
sections.content:
A well-known URI is a URI whose path component begins with the characters /.well-known/, and whose scheme is HTTP, HTTPS, or another scheme that has explicitly been specified to use well-known URIs. Applications that wish to mint new well-known URIs MUST register them.

The example the RFC gives: if an application registers the name example, the corresponding well-known URI on http://www.example.com/ is http://www.example.com/.well-known/example. Registered names MUST conform to the segment-nz production of RFC 3986.

The RFC is careful about what it does not settle. It defines neither how to determine the authority to use for a particular context, nor the scope of the metadata discovered by dereferencing the well-known URI; both should be defined by the application itself.

Typically a registration will reference a specification that defines the format and the associated media type to be obtained by dereferencing the well-known URI. It may also contain additional information, such as the syntax of additional path components, query strings or fragment identifiers to be appended to the well-known URI, or protocol-specific details such as how HTTP methods are handled.

One thing the RFC says plainly: it does not define a format or media type for the resource located at /.well-known/ itself, and clients should not expect a resource to exist at that location.
sections.plainLanguage: A well-known URI is a path that starts with the reserved prefix, on a web address or on a scheme that has been declared to use the same convention. The name after the prefix has to be registered, and the registration normally points at the document that says what the file contains.

sections.title: The Registry and How to Register
sections.content:
The RFC establishes the well-known URI registry. Well-known URIs are registered on the advice of one or more Designated Experts appointed by the IESG or its delegate, with a Specification Required. To allow values to be allocated before publication, the Designated Experts may approve a registration once they are satisfied that such a specification will be published.

Registration requests should be sent to the wellknown-uri-review@ietf.org mailing list for review and comment, with an appropriate subject. Before a period of 14 days has passed, the Designated Experts will either approve or deny the request, communicating the decision both to the review list and to IANA. Denials should include an explanation and, where it applies, suggestions on how to make the request successful. Requests that stay undetermined for longer than 21 days can be brought to the IESG's attention for resolution.

The registration template has four fields. The URI suffix is the name requested for the well-known URI, relative to /.well-known/, for example example. The change controller is IETF for Standards Track RFCs and otherwise the name of the responsible party, with other details such as a postal address, e-mail address or home page URI optionally included. The specification document field references the document that specifies the field, preferably including a URI that can be used to retrieve a copy, with an indication of the relevant sections optional. The related information field optionally carries citations to additional documents with further relevant information.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering a name needs a specification to point at, a named person or group in charge of it, and a note of any other documents that help. A reviewer checks the request and approves or refuses it within a fortnight.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify the scope of applicability of metadata or policy obtained from a well-known URI, and does not specify how to discover a well-known URI for a particular application. Individual applications using the mechanism must define both aspects.

Applications minting new well-known URIs, and administrators deploying them, need to consider several security-related issues, including, but not limited to, exposure of sensitive data, denial-of-service attacks in addition to normal load issues, server and client authentication, vulnerability to DNS rebinding attacks, and attacks in which limited access to a server grants the ability to affect how well-known URIs are served.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing a file at a predictable address has its own risks: the file might reveal something, or be a target for flooding, and the scheme as a whole says nothing about who is allowed to read it. Each application that uses it has to decide those things for itself.

viz.caption: WHAT THE WELL-KNOWN PREFIX IS FOR, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

items.title: For site-wide metadata
items.text: To make policy or other information about a site discoverable before a request is made, when other mechanisms would be too slow or too hard to deploy.

items.title: Not for general retrieval
items.text: Well-known URIs are not intended for general information retrieval or for establishing large URI namespaces on the web.

items.title: A sandbox for collisions
items.text: Reserving one prefix and registering the names inside it keeps two specifications from choosing the same path and keeps them from landing on an existing page.

items.title: Nothing at the prefix itself
items.text: No format or media type is defined for a resource at /.well-known/, and clients should not expect one to exist there.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FIELDS OF A REGISTRATION

cells: The name requested for the well-known URI, relative to /.well-known/, for example example
IETF for Standards Track RFCs, otherwise the name of the responsible party
Reference to the document that specifies the field, preferably with a URI that can retrieve it
Optional citations to additional documents containing further relevant information
